analysis.evidence: שָׂרֵי פַרְעֹה means “Pharaoh’s officials.” They are the subject of both plural verbs וַיִּרְאוּ and וַיְהַלְלוּ. They saw the woman and praised her to Pharaoh.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, masculine plural construct. The following name פַרְעֹה completes the construct phrase.

evidence.note: שָׂרֵי פַרְעֹה identifies the men who see Sarai as Pharaoh’s officials.

article.name: פַּרְעֹה
article.summary: Pharaoh is the royal title by which the text names the king of Egypt. In Abram’s time, Pharaoh’s officials see Sarai and praise her to him.

draft.change: Add a name entry for the royal title פַּרְעֹה and correct the supplied gloss “lye; potash” for this occurrence.
draft.definition: Pharaoh, the title used to designate the king of Egypt.
draft.evidence: Genesis 12:15 identifies Pharaoh through his officials and his household. Exodus 6:11 explicitly calls him פַּרְעֹה מֶלֶךְ מִצְרָיִם, “Pharaoh king of Egypt.”

analysis.evidence: שָׂרֵי פַרְעֹה means “Pharaoh’s officials.” The same officials praise Sarai to Pharaoh, and she is taken into Pharaoh’s house. These clauses identify the possessor as the ruler whose officials saw her.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun. The royal title stands as the possessor after the construct plural שָׂרֵי. It has no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: The king of Egypt, designated by his royal title.

analysis.evidence: The officials first saw the woman and then praised her to Pharaoh. The direct object אֹתָהּ identifies her as the person praised, and אֶל פַּרְעֹה identifies Pharaoh as the one they addressed.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וַ marks the narrative sequence. The verb is a Piel wayyiqtol, third-person masculine plural, agreeing with שָׂרֵי פַרְעֹה, Pharaoh’s officials.

analysis.evidence: In וַיְהַלְלוּ אֹתָהּ אֶל פַּרְעֹה, the officials praised her to Pharaoh. אֹתָהּ identifies the woman they praised, and אֶל introduces Pharaoh as the person they addressed.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew preposition with no prefix or suffix.
